opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's something we think about a lot. With autoregressive models, the community has had years, really close to a decade, of collective experience figuring out what works. There's a well-understood recipe: how to set the learning rate schedule, how to scale the data, how to do tokenization, how to do the post-training stages like instruction tuning and RLHF. A lot of that knowledge is folklore that's been refined by thousands of people running experiments at huge scale.

With diffusion language models, we're much earlier on that curve. In some ways the core training objective is actually quite clean. You're learning to denoise, to reverse a corruption process, and there's a nice principled likelihood bound behind it. But there are many more design choices that haven't been settled yet. What's the right noise process for discrete data? Masking versus other kinds of corruption? How do you weight the different noise levels during training? How do you schedule them at inference time? Each of those interacts with the others, and we don't yet have the same body of empirical wisdom telling us which combinations scale well.

Post-training is another big piece. A lot of the alignment and reasoning techniques were designed with left-to-right generation in mind. Reinforcement learning, for example, typically assumes you can compute the probability of a sequence token by token. With diffusion you have to rethink how you do that, because the generation process is different. So there's real research work in adapting those methods rather than just copying them over.

That said, I'd say it's less that diffusion is fundamentally harder to train and more that it's less explored. Every time we've invested the effort, we've found the models respond well to scale, and we get these big advantages in speed and parallel generation. So I'm optimistic that as more people work on it, the recipes will mature quickly, much like they did for autoregressive models, and for diffusion models in images before that.

r001.rationale: The response says diffusion language models are less explored and that their training recipes remain unsettled, but it does not say efforts to make them work remained unsuccessful for years.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it's one of the things people underestimate. Autoregressive models have had, what, close to a decade now of the entire community iterating on them. Every hyperparameter, every scaling law, every trick around learning rate schedules, data mixtures, tokenization, how you do pretraining versus mid-training versus post-training, all of that has been tuned by thousands of people and enormous amounts of compute. So when you start a new autoregressive run, you're standing on this very mature foundation, and you mostly know what's going to happen.

With diffusion language models, we're much earlier in that journey. The core idea, that you're learning to denoise or to reconstruct masked text in parallel rather than predicting one token at a time, is simple to state, but a lot of the recipe doesn't transfer one-to-one. The loss is different, the noise schedule or masking schedule becomes a design choice that doesn't even exist in the autoregressive world, and things like how you weight different noise levels can have a surprisingly large effect on what the model ends up being good at. Even something as basic as how you evaluate during training is trickier, because likelihoods are bounds rather than exact, so you have to be careful about what signal you're actually optimizing against.

That said, I'd say the gap is closing faster than I expected. A lot of the infrastructure, the architectures, the data pipelines, even a good chunk of the post-training machinery, you can reuse. And there's a nice thing where we can actually initialize from or borrow insights from autoregressive models rather than starting from scratch. So it's not that diffusion is fundamentally harder to train, it's that we're doing in a couple of years what took the autoregressive community a much longer time, with far fewer people working on it. What makes it worth it is that the payoff is on the inference side, you get parallel generation, you get much better latency and throughput, and you get this native ability to do things like editing and infilling. For a lot of applications, especially the agentic ones where you're generating a huge amount of text, that trade is very attractive.

r001.rationale: The response says diffusion language models are earlier in their development and that the gap is closing, but it does not say attempts to make them work remained unsuccessful for years.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s significantly harder right now, but part of that is just the difference in how much effort has gone into the two approaches. For autoregressive models, we have a very mature recipe. We have a lot of experience with architectures, optimization, and scaling. With diffusion language models, we’re still figuring out many of those choices.

There are also more degrees of freedom. How do you corrupt the text? How much noise do you add during training? How do you weight the loss at different noise levels? Those choices affect what the model learns, and then you have choices about how to generate text at inference time.

So if you compare a relatively new diffusion recipe against a very well-tuned autoregressive recipe, it’s difficult to separate fundamental differences between the approaches from differences in engineering maturity. I think that’s an important distinction. There’s still a lot to learn about how to train these models well.

r001.rationale: The response says diffusion language model training is still being figured out, but does not say efforts to make them work were unsuccessful for years.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s substantially harder at this point, partly because we have so much more experience with autoregressive models. A lot of work has gone into figuring out the architectures, the optimization, the data mixtures—all the details that make training work well at scale. With diffusion language models, we’re still developing that understanding.

There are also more choices to make. What does the corruption process look like? How much noise do you introduce, and how do you weight the loss at different noise levels? Those choices affect which prediction problems the model spends its capacity learning. An autoregressive model has a very clear task: predict the next token given the previous tokens. In diffusion, you’re training across many different levels of corruption.

So when a diffusion model underperforms, it can be difficult to tell whether you’re seeing a limitation of the approach or simply a training recipe that isn’t as mature yet. I think that makes it an interesting research problem, but it also makes clean comparisons challenging.

r001.rationale: The response says diffusion language model training recipes are less mature and still being developed, but it does not say efforts remained unsuccessful for years.
